name: Numbers, Text & Time
description: Floating point, integer overflow, endianness, Unicode and time zones — the representation bugs that ship to production.

modules.name: Numbers & Bits
modules.description: IEEE-754, two's complement, overflow and bitwise fundamentals.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. Compare floats with a tolerance (`math.isclose`), never with `==`. Money belongs in integer minor units or a decimal type, never a float.

cards.prompt: How is an IEEE-754 double laid out, and what special values does it have?
cards.answer: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 stored mantissa bits (53 with the implicit leading 1). Specials: ±0, ±Infinity, and NaN — which is not equal to itself.
cards.explanation: That gives ~15–17 significant decimal digits and exact integers only up to 2^53. `NaN != NaN` is why `Number.isNaN` and `math.isnan` exist, and why NaN in a sort comparator can corrupt the ordering.

cards.prompt: Why do computers use two's complement for signed integers?
cards.answer: Because addition, subtraction and comparison work identically for signed and unsigned values — no separate circuitry, and only one representation of zero.
cards.explanation: The asymmetry is the consequence: an 8-bit range is −128..127, so `-INT_MIN` overflows. In C/C++ signed overflow is undefined behaviour the optimiser exploits; in Java and Rust release builds it wraps; in Rust debug builds it panics.

cards.prompt: Where does integer overflow become a security problem, not just a wrong number?
cards.answer: In size calculations: `malloc(count * size)` can wrap to a small allocation while the code then writes `count * size` bytes — a heap overflow. Length checks that overflow are a classic exploit primitive.
cards.explanation: Use checked arithmetic (`__builtin_mul_overflow`, `checked_mul`, `Math.addExact`) wherever a value derives from untrusted input and feeds a size, index or offset. CWE-190 tracks this class.

cards.prompt: What is endianness, and where must you care?
cards.answer: The byte order of multi-byte values: little-endian stores the least significant byte first (x86, ARM by default), big-endian the most significant first. It matters for binary file formats, network protocols and casting byte buffers.
cards.explanation: Network byte order is big-endian, hence `htons`/`ntohl`. Within one process it is invisible — until you memcpy a struct into a socket or read a file written on another architecture. Serialise explicitly rather than dumping raw structs.

cards.prompt: `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so `x & (x - 1) == 0` tests whether x is a power of ___.
cards.answer: two
cards.explanation: Other staples: `x & -x` isolates the lowest set bit; `x >> 1` is a floor-divide by two for unsigned values; XOR swaps and finds the unique element; and `x & (n-1)` replaces `x % n` when n is a power of two — which is why hash tables use power-of-two capacities.

modules.name: Text & Time
modules.description: Unicode, encodings, and the time-zone rules that break naive date handling.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between a code point, a character and a byte in UTF-8?
cards.answer: A code point is a Unicode number (U+1F600). UTF-8 encodes each code point in 1–4 bytes. A user-perceived character (grapheme cluster) may be several code points — 'é' can be one, or 'e' plus a combining accent.
cards.explanation: This is why `len(s)` differs by language, why slicing by byte index corrupts text, and why an emoji with a skin-tone modifier and ZWJ can be one grapheme made of many code points. Iterate by grapheme when the unit is 'what the user sees'.

resources.title: Joel on Software — The absolute minimum every developer must know about Unicode

cards.prompt: Two usernames look identical but compare as different strings. What is happening and what do you do?
cards.answer: They differ in Unicode normalisation form — composed (NFC) versus decomposed (NFD), or confusable characters. Normalise to NFC (or NFKC for identifiers) before storing and comparing, and apply a confusables/skeleton check for security-sensitive names.
cards.explanation: Without normalisation you get duplicate accounts and failed lookups; without confusable checks you get homograph attacks, where a Cyrillic 'а' impersonates a Latin 'a' in a domain or username.

cards.prompt: How should you store timestamps, and when is UTC the wrong answer?
cards.answer: Store instants as UTC (or with an explicit offset). UTC is wrong for *future* local events — a 9am meeting next March must store the local time plus the IANA zone, because the offset can change before then.
cards.explanation: Time zone rules change by political decision several times a year, so an offset captured today may be wrong for a future date. Keep the tz database updated, never store an abbreviation such as 'CST' (it is ambiguous), and let a library do the arithmetic.

cards.prompt: What is wrong with adding 86,400 seconds to get 'tomorrow'?
cards.answer: Not every local day is 24 hours — DST transitions make them 23 or 25. Adding a day is a calendar operation on local time, not an addition of seconds to an instant.
cards.explanation: Other classics: a local time that does not exist (spring forward) or occurs twice (fall back), leap years, and the assumption that a year has 365 days. Use the calendar API of a real date library and let it resolve ambiguity explicitly.

cards.prompt: The ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 timestamp `2026-09-10T14:30:00Z` uses `Z` to mean ___.
cards.answer: UTC
cards.explanation: 'Z' is Zulu — zero offset. ISO 8601 sorts lexicographically in chronological order, which is why it is the right format for log lines, filenames and API payloads. Locale formats such as 03/04/2026 are ambiguous by design.

resources.title: RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet

modules.name: Bases, Bits & Encodings
modules.description: Binary, hex and octal, bitwise operators, base64, hashing versus encoding, decimals and fixed point.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
n = 255
print(n, format(n, 'x'), bin(n), oct(n))
print(int('2a', 16))
cards.explanation: The same number in decimal, hexadecimal (base 16), binary (base 2) and octal (base 8). One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is two hex digits — which is why memory addresses, colours (`#ff8800`) and hashes are written in hex. `int(s, base)` parses any of them.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `&` keeps bits set in both, `|` bits set in either, `^` bits set in exactly one, `~x` flips every bit (which in two's complement equals −x − 1), `<<` multiplies by powers of two and `>>` floor-divides by them. Bit flags — permissions, feature sets — combine with `|` and test with `&`.

resources.title: Python docs — Bitwise operations on integer types

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
aGk=
4
cards.explanation: Base64 maps every 3 bytes to 4 ASCII characters (6 bits each), padding with `=` — so output is about 33% larger than the input. It exists to carry binary data through text-only channels (JSON, email, data URLs), and provides no secrecy at all: anyone can decode it.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
from decimal import Decimal
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2'))
print(Decimal(0.1 + 0.2))
cards.explanation: `Decimal` does exact base-10 arithmetic, so 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3 — but only when built from strings. `Decimal(0.1 + 0.2)` faithfully records the binary float's exact value, error included. Construct from strings (or integers), and set rounding explicitly for money.

resources.title: Python docs — decimal — Decimal fixed point and floating point arithmetic

cards.prompt: How should an application store and calculate money?
cards.answer: As integers in the smallest unit (cents, pence) or with a decimal type, always paired with a currency code. Never binary floats. Round only at defined points using an explicit rule (banker's rounding or half-up, as the domain requires), and allocate remainders deliberately when splitting.
cards.explanation: Splitting £100 three ways cannot give three equal pence amounts — someone gets the extra penny, and the code must decide who. Currencies have different minor units (JPY has none, some have three), so the precision belongs with the currency, not in a global constant.

cards.prompt: This loop never terminates. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: 0.1 is not exactly representable, so repeatedly adding it never produces exactly 1.0 — `x` goes from 0.9999999999999999 to 1.0999999999999999 and skips the target. Loop on an integer counter (`for i in range(10): x = i / 10`) or compare with `<` or a tolerance.
cards.explanation: Floating-point errors accumulate with every operation. Use `math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9)` for equality, and prefer integer counters for loop control. Summing many floats? `math.fsum` compensates for the lost low-order bits.

resources.title: Python docs — Floating point arithmetic: issues and limitations

modules.name: Text & Time II
modules.description: UTF-16 and surrogate pairs, character sets, epoch time and the year-2038 problem.

cards.prompt: In JavaScript, what does this print?
cards.explanation: JavaScript strings are UTF-16: characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as most emoji, take two code units (a surrogate pair), so `.length` says 2. Spreading or `for...of` iterates code points. A flag or family emoji is several code points joined — `Intl.Segmenter` counts graphemes, which is what users perceive.

cards.prompt: A user's name "José" shows up as "JosÃ©". What happened, and how do you prevent it?
cards.answer: UTF-8 bytes were decoded as Latin-1 (Windows-1252): é is two bytes in UTF-8, each shown as a separate Latin-1 character. Use UTF-8 end to end — declare it explicitly when reading files, in HTTP `Content-Type` charsets, and in database and connection settings.
cards.explanation: This garbling is called mojibake. Every boundary where bytes become text needs a declared encoding; relying on a platform default is how the same code works on one machine and breaks on another. MySQL's legacy `utf8` holds only three bytes per character — use `utf8mb4` for emoji.

cards.prompt: What is Unix time, and what is the year-2038 problem?
cards.answer: Seconds elapsed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, ignoring leap seconds. Stored in a signed 32-bit integer, it overflows on 2038-01-19 at 03:14:07 UTC and wraps to December 1901.
cards.explanation: Modern 64-bit systems use a 64-bit `time_t`, but 32-bit embedded devices, file formats, database columns and protocols still carry 32-bit timestamps. Watch the unit too: JavaScript and Java use milliseconds, Unix APIs seconds — mixing them puts dates in 1970 or the far future.

cards.prompt: Why should you measure durations with a monotonic clock rather than the wall clock?
cards.answer: The wall clock can jump backwards or forwards — NTP corrections, manual changes, leap-second handling — so `end - start` can come out negative or wildly wrong. A monotonic clock only moves forward at a steady rate, which is what elapsed time needs.
cards.explanation: Use `time.monotonic()` / `perf_counter()` in Python, `performance.now()` in browsers, `System.nanoTime()` in Java, `time.Since` in Go (which uses the monotonic reading `time.Now` carries), and `Stopwatch` in .NET. Wall-clock time is for timestamps shown to humans or stored, never for timeouts and benchmarks.
